speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you have a pruritic rash on both of your upper arms; tell me, when did this rash first appear, and have you noticed any new soaps, detergents, or plants recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient complains of a pruritic rash on both upper extremities that has been present for 5 months. She notes that the rash occasionally worsens but has not completely resolved at any point. She denies any recent illnesses and mentions that she has not started any new medications or come into contact with any new substances that she is aware of.

speaker: Doctor
text: The rash has persisted for five months despite your lack of exposure to new triggers. Given the chronic nature and bilateral distribution, do you recall any recent sun exposure or outdoor activities, and does the itching worsen at night?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pruritic rash on the bilateral upper extremities. I also have No fever, No joint pains, No recent illnesses.

speaker: Doctor
text:
You mention no fever or joint pain, which is helpful. To narrow this down, do you notice that the rash appears or gets worse specifically when you are exposed to sunlight?

REQUEST TEST: Complete_Blood_Count; REQUEST TEST: Liver_Function_Tests

speaker: Doctor
text: The blood work and liver function tests are normal, which is good news. Do you notice that the rash becomes red, swollen, or itchy immediately after stepping out in the sun, and does it fade or disappear once you go back inside?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No history of serious illness. No known drug allergies. Takes no medications. Social history: College student studying graphic design. Non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially. No recreational drug use.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is helpful context; your occupation as a graphic design student makes sun exposure a significant possibility. To confirm my suspicion, does the rash appear as distinct, reddish-purple spots on the sun-exposed parts of your arms, and do they fade after you stop being in the sun?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Polymorphous Light Eruption (PMLE)
